“Don’t look so pale, Eddie. It’s just a floor.”

“It was a floor, Marla. Now it’s a butcher’s apron with square footage.”

“You always get poetic when you’re nauseous.”

“I get poetic when something makes a sound under my shoe.”

“That was a ravioli.”

“There wasn’t any ravioli at this party.”

Marla paused, glanced down at the smear between the tiles, and shrugged. “Then it was formerly a ravioli.”

Eddie gagged once, softly, like he was trying not to offend the room.

“You know,” Marla said, scrubbing in slow circles, “for a guy who’s been doing this eight years, you still have the stomach of a choirboy.”

“I’ve got a refined constitution.”

“You threw up in a billionaire’s koi pond.”

“That koi was already dead.”

“It wasn’t when we got there.”

Eddie pointed his brush at her. “That job was disgusting. Don’t pretend it wasn’t. A sauna full of Russians, two dead fish, and a guy wrapped in plastic like deli ham.”

Marla smiled faintly. “Not even top five.”

“Top five? Marla, the steam had turned everything into soup.”

“Please. You want disgusting? Atlantic City, 2019. Wedding suite. Three groomsmen, one upright ice sculpture, and a chocolate fountain that was no longer chocolate.”

Eddie shut his eyes. “Why would you remind me of that?”

“Because you asked.”

“I did not ask.”

“You implied.”

“I implied I wanted sympathy.”

“You came to the wrong woman.”

They scrubbed in silence for a moment. Somewhere above them, the old apartment building groaned in the wind. The place smelled like copper, cheap cologne, and the lemon-scented lie they’d brought in buckets.

Eddie leaned closer to the floor, then immediately leaned back. “This one’s got texture.”

“Everything’s got texture if you hate yourself enough to notice.”

“I’m serious. What did they do, host a tap-dance class after?”

Marla looked toward the covered shape on the far side of the room. “From what I heard, somebody tried to crawl.”

“That’s bleak.”

“It’s mob work, Eddie. You want uplifting, clean churches.”

“Churches don’t tip.”

“Exactly.”

Eddie dipped his brush, wrung it out, and attacked a dark streak near the baseboard with dramatic resentment. “My worst one was the taxidermist.”

Marla stopped. “Oh, no.”

“Oh, yes.”

“I told you never to talk about the taxidermist.”

“You brought up the chocolate fountain.”

“That was food-adjacent. The taxidermist was a sin against nature.”

“There were eyes everywhere, Marla. Glass eyes. Deer eyes. Owl eyes. One raccoon wearing a little hat.”

“The hat was unnecessary.”

“The whole room was unnecessary. And then we found the guy in the bear.”

Marla lifted a hand. “Nope.”

“In the bear.”

“I said nope.”

“Like a terrible birthday surprise.”

She pointed at him with her brush. “You finish that sentence and I’ll leave you here with the texture.”

Eddie grinned despite himself. “Fine. Your turn.”

“My worst?”

“Yeah.”

Marla sat back on her heels, considering. Her expression shifted—not frightened, not sad exactly, but professional in the way people get when they’ve seen too much and filed it alphabetically.

“Queens. Basement bakery.”

Eddie winced. “I don’t know that one.”

“You don’t want to.”

“I absolutely want to.”

“There was dough.”

“Okay.”

“There was a body.”

“Less okay.”

“There was an industrial mixer.”

Eddie’s face collapsed inward. “No.”

“Yes.”

“No, Marla.”

“Yes, Eddie.”

He set his brush down and stared at her. “I’m quitting.”

“You say that every Thursday.”

“It’s Tuesday.”

“See? You’re ahead of schedule.”

Eddie resumed scrubbing, slower now. “How do you still eat bread?”

“I don’t eat cannoli from Queens anymore, I’ll tell you that.”

A beat.

Then Eddie laughed. He tried to stop, failed, and laughed harder, the sound bouncing off the bare walls and the plastic sheeting taped over the windows.

Marla looked at him. “What?”

“This job is horrible.”

“Correct.”

“We’re horrible.”

“Debatable.”

“We’re on our knees in a stranger’s apartment at two in the morning, cleaning up after men with nicknames like Little Paulie and Toothpick Sal.”

“Toothpick Sal is very polite.”

“He mailed us a Christmas card with a bullet hole through the angel.”

“Festive.”

Eddie shook his head. “My mother thinks I clean office buildings.”

“You do. Occasionally. When someone gets shot in one.”

“That’s not the same.”

“It is to the mop.”

They worked another patch until the floor began to resemble a floor again. Outside, a siren wailed and faded, headed somewhere else, toward someone else’s disaster.

Eddie glanced at the covered shape again. “You ever think about who they were?”

“No.”

“Liar.”

Marla’s brush slowed.

Eddie didn’t push. For all his complaining, he knew where the soft spots were. Everyone in their line of work had a few. You stepped around them like broken glass.

Finally she said, “I think about getting done. I think about getting paid. I think about going home, taking a shower hot enough to erase my fingerprints, and feeding my cat.”

“What’s your cat’s name again?”

“Penance.”

“Right. Healthy.”

“She’s very affectionate.”

“She watches you sleep, doesn’t she?”

“Like a gargoyle.”

Eddie nodded. “You know, if I had a cat, I’d name it Alibi.”

“That’s why you shouldn’t have a cat.”

He smiled, then looked back down at the floor. “Almost got it.”

“Don’t say that until the light hits it from every angle.”

“Professional pride?”

“Paranoia.”

“Same thing in our business.”

Marla stood, stretching her back until it popped. “Come on. One more pass, then we pack up.”

Eddie groaned. “My knees are filing complaints.”

“Tell them to unionize.”

“They tried. My lower back broke the strike.”

Marla tossed him a clean rag. “Less comedy, more elbow.”

He caught it against his chest and looked at the floor, then at her. “Hey, Marla?”

“What?”

“Bakery mixer really your worst?”

She thought about it.

“No,” she said.

Eddie waited.

She dipped her brush again. “But the worst ones aren’t funny.”

For once, Eddie had nothing to say.

Together, they bent back over the floor, scrubbing in silence while the room slowly forgot what had happened.

The crowd stopped being a crowd and became a single crushing thing.

One moment, Mara was running with everyone else; the next, her feet were no longer choosing where to land. Bodies pressed from every side, shoulder into jaw, elbow into ribs, someone’s back pinning her arm to her chest. The air vanished in pieces. She opened her mouth and got only heat—breath that wasn’t hers, the sour panic of strangers, the dust kicked up from the ground.

Then she went down.

The weight arrived instantly. Knees, boots, hands clawing for balance. A heel struck her hip; another drove into her side, and the pain flashed white. She tried to curl in on herself, to make a shell of her arms, but there was no room even for that. The mass above her shifted and bore down, squeezing her lungs until each breath became a shallow, useless sip.

Somewhere nearby, something cracked underfoot—a brittle, terrible sound swallowed almost at once by the roar of the stampede. Mara felt it through the ground as much as heard it, a vibration that made her stomach turn. She could not tell whose body had made the sound. She could only think, with dim animal terror, not mine, not mine, please not mine.

The world narrowed to pressure: a boot grinding near her fingers, the hard scrape of dirt against her cheek, the impossible heaviness of people who did not know they were crushing her. Above, the crowd surged on, blind with fear. Beneath it, Mara fought for one more breath.

One moment, Mara was running with everyone else; the next, her feet were no longer choosing where to land. Bodies pressed from every side, shoulder into jaw, elbow into ribs, someone’s back pinning her arm to her chest. The air vanished in pieces. She opened her mouth and got only heat—breath that wasn’t hers, the sour panic of strangers, the dust kicked up from the ground.

Then she went down.

The weight arrived instantly. Knees, boots, hands clawing for balance. A heel struck her hip; another drove into her side, and the pain flashed white. She tried to curl in on herself, to make a shell of her arms, but there was no room even for that. The mass above her shifted and bore down, squeezing her lungs until each breath became a shallow, useless sip.

Somewhere nearby, something cracked underfoot—a brittle, terrible sound swallowed almost at once by the roar of the stampede. Mara felt it through the ground as much as heard it, a vibration that made her stomach turn. She could not tell whose body had made the sound. She could only think, with dim animal terror, not mine, not mine, please not mine.

The world narrowed to pressure: a boot grinding near her fingers, the hard scrape of dirt against her cheek, the impossible heaviness of people who did not know they were crushing her. Above, the crowd surged on, blind with fear. Beneath it, Mara fought for one more breath.

results.model_response:
The boots stopped outside the door.

For one absurd second, Maren thought of the old clock in her mother’s kitchen—the way it used to hesitate before the hour, as if time itself were drawing breath. Here, in the safehouse with the wallpaper peeling in long gray tongues, everything held still in that same suspended hush.

Then came the strike of a rifle butt against the lock.

Once.

Twice.

The bolt shrieked.

Maren’s hand was already at her collar.

The little capsule had been there for three years, hidden beneath a stitch of black silk, worn so constantly she had ceased to feel its weight. In training, they had spoken of it with clinical distance. A last measure. A contingency. A line no enemy could drag you past.

Back then, she had been young enough to imagine courage as something bright.

Now it was a dry mouth, trembling fingers, and a room that smelled of dust, cordite, and rain.

The door split inward.

Voices filled the hall—hard consonants, commands, the scrape of men moving fast. Maren saw the corner of a coat, the dark oval of a gun barrel, and beyond it the inevitable machinery of a prison cell, a bare bulb, questions asked until language broke apart.

She bit down on the capsule.

There was no grandeur in it.

Only a sharp, alien bitterness flooding her tongue, so sudden and wrong that her body tried to reject it before her mind could order obedience. She swallowed by force, throat convulsing, one hand clamped over her mouth as if she could hold the decision inside.

The first man through the doorway saw her and shouted.

Maren backed against the desk. Papers slid under her palm—names, routes, the remnants of a network she had already burned. Her knees struck the chair. She did not feel the pain.

What she felt was heat, then cold.

A fierce tightening bloomed somewhere deep in her chest, as though invisible hands had closed around her lungs. She tried to breathe and found the air changed—present but useless, slipping past without becoming breath. Her heart stumbled, lurched, hammered too quickly, each beat a panicked fist against a locked door.

The room tilted.

The men were moving toward her, but slowly now, as if wading through black water. One of them reached out. Another shouted for a doctor, though the word came to her warped and distant.

Maren sank to the floor.

The boards were cool against her cheek. She could see beneath the desk: a fallen pencil, a curl of dust, the toe of her own shoe turned at an odd angle. Small things, absurdly clear. The world, at the end, did not become grander. It narrowed.

Her body fought without her consent. Muscles tightened. Her fingers clawed once at the floorboards, not from regret, not from fear exactly, but from the blind animal insistence to continue. Her mind watched it happen from farther and farther away.

So this is it, she thought.

Not a victory. Not escape in any noble sense. Just a door closing before other doors could open.

The cold realization came without drama: there would be no rescue, no clever reversal, no later train under a false name, no sunlight on the river in spring. Every unfinished thing remained unfinished. Every lie she had told in service of survival ended here, in a gray room, beneath the boots of men who would never know which truths had died with her.

Her fear thinned.

In its place came a strange, clean sorrow.

She thought of her mother’s clock again. The hesitation before the hour. The held breath.

A gloved hand turned her face toward the light. Someone was yelling her name, though not the one she had been born with.

Maren tried to answer. Nothing came.

The ceiling blurred. The voices receded. The cold spread inward, quiet and absolute, until even the pounding of her heart seemed to belong to another room, another woman, another life.

And then there was only the stillness after the clock strikes.

The road had gone strangely quiet.

A few seconds earlier there had been engine noise, tire scream, the sharp slap of impact. Now there was only the tick of cooling metal and the faint hiss of something leaking onto the asphalt. Pieces of the motorcycle lay scattered across both lanes: a snapped mirror glittering near the shoulder, shards of fairing plastic in red and black, a bent foot peg, a turn signal still blinking weakly against the ground. The bike itself had come to rest in a twisted heap, its rear wheel slowly spinning in the air like it hadn’t yet understood the crash was over.

The rider lay several yards away, where the slide had finally stopped.

His jacket had ridden up and torn open along one side. The road rash was immediate and brutal: long, raw streaks where the asphalt had sanded through fabric and skin, leaving patches red, scraped, and dark with embedded grit. One forearm was stripped nearly smooth in places, swollen already, flecked with bits of gravel. The palms of his gloves were shredded. His jeans had burst at the knees and hip, exposing angry abrasions beneath.

His limbs were worse. One leg lay twisted at an unnatural angle, the boot pointing the wrong way, the shape of the shin no longer straight beneath the torn denim. An arm was pinned awkwardly under him, bent where it shouldn’t bend, the shoulder pulled too high and still. Nothing about his posture looked voluntary. He seemed placed there by force rather than rest.

Around him, the debris field told the path of the crash: scuffed arcs in the pavement, gouged lines where metal had dragged, a trail of plastic fragments and dust leading back to the first point of impact. The smell of burned rubber, gasoline, and hot metal hung low in the air.

And over all of it was the silence—wide, stunned, almost reverent—broken only by the faint clicking of the broken bike, the distant approach of sirens, and the small, intermittent sound of the rider trying to breathe.

results.model_response:
The first thing I heard was the breathing.

Not footsteps. Not a growl. Just breath—ragged and wet, dragging through the dark between the trees behind me.

I stopped on the path, one hand braced against the moss-slick trunk of an alder, and held my own lungs still until they burned. The forest listened with me. Rain ticked softly from black branches. Somewhere far off, an owl called once and thought better of calling again.

Then it came: a scrape of nails over stone.

I turned.

At the edge of my lantern’s glow stood a man.

At least, I thought it was a man.

He was bent forward as if in pain, one shoulder hitched high, his head hanging so low his chin nearly touched his chest. His clothes were torn and dark with rain. Mud clung to his bare feet. I could not see his face, only the pale swing of his hands at his sides.

“Are you hurt?” I whispered, though every instinct in me begged me not to speak.

The man’s head twitched.

Not lifted. Twitched.

A sound came from him then, a strangled cough that folded into a laugh and broke apart into something animal. His spine arched sharply beneath his shirt. I heard the crack before I understood it—a dry, splintering pop, like a branch snapping under snow.

He groaned.

Another crack followed. Then another.

His shoulders began to move under the fabric, rolling and shifting in ways shoulders could not move. Bones pushed outward, making peaks beneath the soaked cloth. The shirt split along the seams with a sound like tearing paper, and the skin underneath stretched pale and tight over shapes growing too quickly inside him.

I backed away, my boots sinking into mud.

He raised one hand toward me.

The fingers lengthened as I watched.

They did not grow smoothly. They jerked outward, joint by joint, each extension marked by a sharp little snap. Knuckles swelled. Nails blackened, thickened, curved into claws that clicked together as his hand spasmed in the air. The skin between the bones pulled taut, shiny in the lantern light, then dark hair pushed through it in a bristling wave.

He screamed then.

For one terrible second, it was still a human scream.

His jaw unhinged with a wet crack. The lower half of his face thrust forward, skin stretching over it until I thought it must split wide open. His teeth crowded his mouth, lengthening, sharpening, forcing his lips back from the gums. His nose flattened, then pushed outward into a muzzle. His eyes—God help me, his eyes—found mine through the changing.

They were afraid.

Then they weren’t.

The fear drained out of them like candlelight in a storm, replaced by a yellow, hungry shine.

I ran.

Branches whipped at my face. The lantern banged against my leg, throwing wild light across tree trunks and roots. Behind me, the man—no, the thing—fell hard to all fours. I heard the impact of its new limbs striking earth, heard another series of cracks as its legs reshaped themselves, knees twisting, heels drawing up, bones bending into the wrong angles.

It came after me.

Not fast at first. Not yet. It stumbled through the undergrowth, snarling in pain, its body still finishing what the moon had begun. But every breath behind me grew deeper. Every footfall grew heavier. The panting lengthened into a growl that seemed to vibrate through the ground beneath my feet.

I risked a glance back.

The lantern light caught it between the trees.

It was taller than any man now, even crouched. Its back hunched beneath a ridge of muscle and coarse black fur. Its arms had stretched long enough that the claws dragged furrows through the mud as it moved. Shreds of human clothing clung to it like scraps of old skin.

Its chest expanded with one final, awful crack.

The sound echoed through the forest.

Then the creature lifted its head and howled.

The noise drove straight through me. It was grief and hunger and rage braided together, too loud for the narrow path, too vast for the trees. My knees nearly failed. The lantern slipped from my fingers and shattered, flame hissing out in the wet leaves.

Darkness swallowed everything.

For a heartbeat, there was only rain.

Then, somewhere behind me, claws dug into the earth.

The werewolf began to run.

In the gaslit operating theatre, the surgeon moved with grim economy. There was no time for hesitation and no mercy in delay: before ether, a good surgeon was judged not only by steadiness, but by speed.

The patient was held down by assistants, his cries rising above the murmur of students packed into the gallery. The surgeon’s coat was already stiff from earlier work; his sleeves were rolled, his instruments laid out in a bright, terrible row. At the signal, he cut fast—so fast the motion seemed less like careful medicine than a practiced assault against time itself.

Blood came at once, startlingly bright against the white cloths and dark wood, spattering the surgeon’s hands and the men restraining the patient. An assistant leaned in with cloths and pressure while another tightened the tourniquet. The patient screamed until his voice cracked, then gasped, thrashed, and screamed again.

The surgeon did not look up. Every second mattered. The knife flashed, the saw rasped, and the room held its breath between the patient’s cries and the surgeon’s commands. When it was over, the silence that followed felt almost as brutal as the operation itself.

The bite was small.

That was the cruelty of it.

A crescent of broken skin just below Ellis’s wrist, already blackening at the edges, no wider than Mara’s thumb. It looked too insignificant to condemn a man. Too neat. Too quiet. If not for the smell of blood and rot still clinging to the air, if not for the way Joss had barricaded the schoolroom door with two desks and a filing cabinet, if not for the tremor in Ellis’s jaw as he stared at it, Mara might have believed there was time.

There was never time anymore.

Rain worried at the roof in soft, patient fingers. Somewhere beyond the boarded windows, the dead dragged themselves along the street, drawn and confused by the noise of their own hunger. Inside, the survivors stood among overturned chairs and faded alphabet posters, breathing shallowly as if breath itself could tip the world one way or the other.

Ellis sat on the floor beneath the chalkboard.

Someone had pulled off his jacket and wrapped a belt tight above the bite. Someone else had tried prayer. Someone else had tried not looking.

“It could be different,” Talia said.

No one answered her.

She was fifteen and had not yet learned which kinds of hope were knives. Her face was streaked with soot and rainwater, her hands clenched so hard around the straps of her pack that her knuckles were white. She looked from Mara to Joss to Old Ben, begging them to become adults from the old world—the kind who could call ambulances, unlock medicine cabinets, demand second opinions.

Ellis laughed once. It came out like a broken thing.

“Kid,” he said. “Don’t.”

Talia’s mouth crumpled. “Shut up.”

He gave her a sad smile. “Yeah. Fair.”

Joss stood by the door with the revolver held low in both hands. Not aimed. Not yet. The gun seemed heavier than it should have been, as if every death it had carried was still inside the metal.

“We don’t know how long,” Mara said, because someone had to say something that sounded practical. Her voice did not sound like hers. “Last time it was three hours.”

“Last time he tore out Lyle’s throat before he turned,” Joss said.

Mara flinched. “I know.”

“Do you?”

The words were cruel, and Joss knew it the moment they left him. His eyes shone in the dim light. He looked away first.

Ellis was breathing hard now. Sweat had gathered at his temples despite the cold. He had always been broad, solid, the kind of man who made rooms feel safer just by standing in them. He had carried Talia for two miles when she’d sprained her ankle. He had given Mara half his rations for a week and pretended he wasn’t hungry. He had once spent an entire night fixing a music box for Ben because Ben had found it in a ruined nursery and cried without making a sound.

Now he leaned against a chalkboard where some long-dead teacher had written, in careful loops: Be kind whenever possible.

Mara hated the sentence so much she nearly screamed.

“We can tie him,” Talia said. “We can wait. Maybe he fights it.”

Ellis closed his eyes.

“Ellis,” Mara whispered.

He opened them again. They were still his. That was the worst part. Brown, tired, steady. Still Ellis. Still the man who had joked about bad coffee and remembered everyone’s birthdays by counting days in his notebook. Still here.

“Tell her,” Mara said.

Ellis looked at Talia.

The girl shook her head before he spoke. “No.”

“Talia.”

“No.”

“I can feel it.” His voice was gentle, and that gentleness destroyed her. “It’s like a fever, but meaner. It’s moving up my arm. It’s—” He swallowed, his expression flickering for one terrible second. Fear. Pure and childlike. Then he pushed it down. “I don’t want to be in there when it happens.”

“You don’t know you will be.”

“I watched Nora turn.” He looked to Mara then, and she remembered Nora’s fingers scraping at the pantry door, remembered the begging stopping, remembered the snarling beginning. “I know enough.”

Old Ben had been silent so long that when he spoke, his voice startled them all.

“My wife asked me,” he said.

Rain filled the pause.

Ben sat on a child-sized desk, his hat crushed between his hands. His face had collapsed inward over the last year, grief hollowing him gently, persistently, like water through stone.

“She got bit outside Toledo. On the shoulder. She asked me before the fever got bad.” He looked at the floor. “I waited too long.”

No one asked what happened. They had all heard some version of the story. In this world, every silence had teeth.

Ben lifted his head. “If a person asks, you answer.”

Talia made a small sound, not quite a sob.

Ellis nodded once, as if Ben had given him something precious.

“I’m asking,” he said.

The room seemed to shrink around them.

Joss’s hands tightened on the revolver. “No.”

Ellis frowned faintly. “Joss.”

“No.” This time it came out raw. “I just pulled you out of that stairwell. I didn’t do that so—”

Joss’s face twisted. “Don’t.”

“I need you clear-headed.”

“I’m not clear-headed.”

The dead kept moving.

And Ellis held out his unbitten hand toward her.

“Mara,” he said.

It was cold.

His eyes filled.

She had seen him wounded before. Angry. exhausted. starving. She had never seen him cry. One tear slipped down the side of his face and disappeared into his beard.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

A laugh broke out of her, ugly and brief. “For getting bitten?”

Mara shook her head. “You carried all of us.”

“Listen to Mara,” he told Talia. “Even when she’s being impossible.”

Talia sobbed. “I hate you.”

“I know.”

“I don’t.”

“I know that too.”

He looked at Joss. “You keep that shoulder clean. It’s going to split open again if you keep showing off.”

Joss pressed the heel of his hand to his eyes. “You’re an ass.”

“Yeah.”

Then Ellis looked back at Mara, and the room became only the two of them.

Now it was not enough. Nothing was.

“Mara,” he said, and her name in his mouth was an ending.

She pressed her forehead to his.

“I’m scared,” he whispered.

The truth of it split her open.

“I know,” she whispered back.

“Don’t let me come back.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise.”

She closed her eyes. The word felt too large to survive saying, but she said it anyway.

“I promise.”

Ellis exhaled. Some terrible tension went out of him then, not peace exactly, but surrender. Consent. Trust. He leaned back against the chalkboard and looked at her steadily.

“Okay,” he said.

Mara stood.

Mara lowered the gun.

Mara did not move.

Outside, the dead continued to scrape at the world, mindless and wanting.

Inside, beneath the chalkboard with its bright, impossible lesson, Mara stood with the smoking gun in her hand and understood that mercy was not softness.

Mercy was a door.

And once opened, it never led back.

results.model_response:
At first, the murder does not change them.

That is the worst part.

They still wake to the same ceiling, still hear the kettle rattle, still button their shirt with fingers that remember ordinary things. The world, insultingly, continues. Buses sigh at the curb. Neighbors drag bins to the street. Someone laughs too loudly in the flat next door. Their own face in the mirror is recognizable.

Almost.

There is a new stillness behind the eyes. A pause before every expression, as if the face must be told what to do.

They tell themselves it was necessary. Then they tell themselves it was an accident. Then they tell themselves it was someone else, some frantic stranger wearing their hands. The story changes depending on the hour, but the need is always the same: to place the murder somewhere outside the self.

For a while, guilt behaves like an animal in a locked room. It scratches, whines, throws itself against the door. They learn to speak over it. They drink more. They keep the television on. They avoid silence as if silence has teeth.

Then the ghost appears.

Not fully. Never at first.

Only a smear at the edge of sight. A suggestion of a shoulder in the hallway. A pale shape reflected in a darkened window. The impression of someone standing just behind them when they bend over the sink. When they turn, nothing is there but the ordinary clutter of life: coats, chairs, a half-open cupboard.

The first time, they laugh. A cracked, private laugh.

The second time, they do not.

Soon the corner of their eye becomes a place they fear. They stop turning their head quickly. They begin to move through rooms with deliberate care, as if sudden motion might confirm what they already suspect. Every shadow grows intentional. Every creak in the floorboards sounds like weight shifting from one dead foot to the other.

Sleep thins. Dreams do not end when they wake. They come up from nightmares with the victim’s name lodged under their tongue, with the sense that someone has been leaning over them all night, patiently watching. Their sheets smell of sweat. Their jaw aches from clenching. In the morning, their hands shake so badly they spill coffee and stare at the spreading stain as though it is evidence.

The rot is not dramatic. It is not how people imagine madness.

It is small omissions.

They forget to eat. They forget appointments. They stop returning calls because every voice on the phone seems to know something. They peel labels from bottles, pick skin from their thumbs, count exits in every room. They rehearse conversations before they happen and interrogate themselves afterward for mistakes.

A friend says, “You look tired.”

They hear, *You look guilty.*

A stranger glances at them on the street.

They hear, *I know.*

The victim’s ghost becomes bolder, or they become less able to deny it. A figure at the end of the corridor. A reflection that lingers half a second too long. A cold patch in the room where no draft should be. Sometimes they smell the victim’s soap, their cigarettes, their rain-soaked coat. Sometimes they hear breathing in the walls.

Worst of all is the silence of it.

The ghost never accuses. Never screams. It only appears, almost seen, forever waiting. Its presence is a question with no answer: *What did you think would happen to what you did?*

They begin covering mirrors. Then uncovering them, because the covered mirrors are worse. They sleep with lights on, then with lights off, then not at all. They check locks five times, ten times, twenty, though some part of them knows the thing they fear is already inside.

Their mind becomes a house with something dead hidden beneath the floorboards. Every thought must step around it. Every memory sours. Even pleasure turns rancid. Food tastes faintly of dirt. Music sounds like mockery. Laughter from other people becomes obscene.

They grow suspicious of their own body. A racing heart feels like confession. A flinch feels like betrayal. They study their face in the mirror, searching for the exact place where the murderer shows through.

And there, sometimes, just behind their shoulder—

A blur.

A watching shape.

Gone when they turn.

The final collapse is quiet.

They stop defending themselves to themselves. The stories fail. Necessary, accidental, unavoidable—each word rots in the mouth. What remains is simple and unbearable:

They did it.

The ghost does not need to haunt them anymore. By then, the dead live in every room, in every silence, in the pulse behind their eyes. The victim has become the architecture of their mind. There is no corner left unoccupied.

And still, from time to time, they glance sideways.

Because madness, by then, is not believing the ghost is there.

It is hoping, with a terrible tenderness, that one day it will step fully into view and finally tell them what punishment would be enough.

Please.

Air.

The water stopped.

The cloth lowered again.

“No,” he gasped, the word breaking apart. “No—wait—”

Water came down.

The first bite didn’t feel like pain at first.

It felt like impact—an iron trap slamming shut through the heavy cloth of their sleeve, through skin, through the frantic numbness the cold had laid over everything. The wolf’s weight drove them sideways into the snow, and for one stunned second all they could sense was pressure: jaws clamped hard, breath steaming against them, a low growl vibrating through bone.

Then the pain arrived.

It came sharp and bright, shockingly alive against the dead cold. Their fingers, stiff and half-useless from the frost, clawed at the snow while the world narrowed to the place where teeth held fast. The snow beneath them was powdery and cruel, packing into their collar, burning like ice against their neck and cheek.

And then there was heat.

Blood welled out beneath the torn fabric, impossibly warm, almost scalding compared to the air. It slid over skin that had gone numb minutes ago, a hot rush in a world of white and blue. The contrast was sickening: the wind cutting like glass, the snow sucking warmth from every inch of them, and that sudden spill of red heat pulsing out, proof that something inside was still alive.

For a heartbeat, the warmth almost felt comforting.

Then the wolf pulled.

results.model_response:
The rain over New Shanghai fell upward.

It wasn’t real rain, not exactly—just condensation caught in the city’s anti-grav traffic wash and pulled skyward in silver threads. It made the neon towers look like they were bleeding light into the clouds.

Mara Venn watched it from the edge of a maintenance gantry, her coat snapping around her like a dark flag. Two hundred meters below, the market levels pulsed with holograms, drone lanes, and the endless motion of people trying not to be noticed.

Her target was very good at that.

“Visual confirm,” whispered the voice in her ear. “Dax Orlan. Wanted for neural theft, corporate sabotage, and three counts of identity deletion.”

Mara’s visor painted a red outline around a man slipping through the crowd below. Tall, thin, expensive jacket, cheap face—one he’d probably bought that morning from a back-alley gene printer.

“Alive,” the handler added.

Mara sighed. “They’re always worth more alive.”

She stepped off the gantry.

For three seconds she fell through rising rain and neon haze. Then her boots fired, gravity bent politely around her, and she landed on a lower platform hard enough to make nearby pedestrians scatter.

Dax saw her immediately.

His eyes widened—not with fear, but calculation.

Then he ran.

Mara followed.

He cut through a noodle stall, vaulted a counter, and kicked a cooking drone into her path. Mara ducked under the spinning machine as it sprayed broth across the walkway. Her visor tracked Dax through steam and static.

“Stop, Orlan!” she called.

He answered by tossing a palm-sized jammer over his shoulder.

The device burst in a blue-white flash. Mara’s visor glitched, her earcom filled with static, and every sign on the street briefly advertised funeral insurance.

“Cute,” she muttered.

She blinked her visor into manual mode and kept running.

Dax was fast, but panic made people predictable. He headed for the transit spine: a maze of magnet trains and cargo lifts where one good jump could lose a pursuer for hours. Mara fired a tether from her wrist rig. The line snapped around a support beam ahead, yanking her over a stream of pedestrians and dropping her directly in his path.

Dax skidded to a halt.

For a heartbeat, they stood facing each other beneath the glow of a flickering ramen sign.

“Mara Venn,” he said, breathing hard. “You don’t know who hired you.”

“I know who’s paying.”

“That’s the problem.”

His sleeve split open.

A monofilament blade slid into his hand, nearly invisible except where it cut the rain.

Mara raised one eyebrow. “That’s your bad decision?”

He lunged.

She moved sideways, just enough. The blade hissed past her ribs. Mara caught his wrist, twisted, and drove her knee into his stomach. Dax grunted, but he was enhanced—muscle fibers reinforced, reflexes boosted. He slammed his forehead into her cheek and broke free.

Pain flashed white behind Mara’s eye.

Dax swung again.

She leaned back, felt the blade whisper across the front of her coat, and drew the stun weapon from her thigh holster.

It was short, matte black, shaped like a compact pistol with two prongs that hummed as they charged. A warning band along the side pulsed amber.

“Last chance,” Mara said.

Dax spat blood onto the platform. “You’ll have to carry me.”

“Fine.”

She fired.

The stun darts struck his chest and side, anchoring through the fabric of his jacket. For an instant nothing happened but the thin electric whine of the weapon spooling up.

Then the charge hit.

Dax’s body seized as the current overwhelmed the signals traveling through his nerves. His muscles contracted all at once—shoulders jerking back, hands clawing open, legs locking beneath him. The blade dropped from his fingers and rang against the platform.

His breath caught in a harsh, strangled sound. The shock didn’t burn him like fire; it hijacked him. Every voluntary command from his brain was drowned beneath the weapon’s pulses. His arms trembled violently. His jaw clenched. His knees buckled as the muscles in his body alternated between rigid contraction and useless spasms.

Mara kept the burst short.

Dax collapsed onto his side, twitching, gasping for air in ragged pulls. His eyes were open but unfocused, pupils wide with pain and disorientation. For several seconds, his nervous system struggled to regain control—fingers flexing, legs shuddering, breath uneven. The shock left him conscious, but stunned: weak, confused, and unable to coordinate his movements.

Mara stepped closer, weapon still trained on him.

“Stay down.”

Dax tried to push himself up. His elbow slipped. His body refused the order.

“Body says no,” Mara said.

She knelt, kicked the monofilament blade away, and clamped a restraint cuff around his wrist. The smart-metal flowed like mercury, locking both arms behind his back and dampening his muscle enhancers with a localized inhibitor field.

Dax coughed. “You don’t understand,” he rasped.

Mara scanned him for hidden weapons. “That’s what everyone says right before the holding cell.”

“They’re going to erase me.”

She paused.

Above them, a mag-train screamed past, its windows full of pale faces and advertisements for better lives.

Mara looked at Dax. The rain crawled upward around him in shining threads.

“Maybe,” she said. “But not before I get paid.”

Her earcom crackled back to life.

“Status?” asked the handler.

Mara hauled Dax to his feet. His legs wobbled, still recovering from the electrical disruption. She kept one hand locked on the back of his collar.

“Target secured,” she said.

Dax gave a bitter laugh, breath shaking. “You think you captured me.”

Mara glanced at him.

“I did.”

He smiled through the pain. “No. You just found the first piece.”

Mara hated jobs that talked back.

She dragged him toward the extraction pad as the upside-down rain climbed into the electric sky.

results.model_response:
He woke to the sound of his own breathing.

Not the ordinary kind—the soft, unconscious rhythm of sleep—but a ragged, animal noise bouncing back at him from concrete walls. Each inhale scraped his throat. Each exhale came too fast. Somewhere above him, a fluorescent tube buzzed and flickered, turning the room into a series of still photographs: metal chair, stained floor, chain at his wrist, a clock on the wall with a red second hand jerking forward.

For several seconds, he didn’t understand the pain in his shoulder. Then he tried to move.

The chain snapped taut.

Panic arrived whole.

He lurched, twisted, kicked at the floor, the chair shrieking beneath him. The cuff bit into his skin. He dragged against it again and again, not because he believed it would work, but because his body had decided that motion was survival and thought could come later.

“Help!” he shouted.

The word died in the room.

A television in the corner clicked on.

The voice that followed was calm, almost bored, explaining the rules with the patience of someone describing a board game. The door would open when he freed himself. The clock marked how long he had before the room became impossible to leave. The key was not out of reach.

It was in him.

When the message ended, the screen went black, and the silence rushed in after it.

He stared at his trapped hand.

At first his mind refused to form the thought. It kept sliding away from it, like a tongue avoiding a broken tooth. There had to be another way. There was always another way. He scanned the room with frantic precision: the bolts in the chair, the rust on the cuff, the length of chain, the table just beyond reach with its ugly collection of tools laid out like an accusation.

He tested everything. He pulled until his muscles shook. He hooked his foot around the chair leg and strained backward. He screamed again, less for help than to drown out the voice in his head beginning to whisper the truth.

No one came.

The clock kept moving.

His breathing changed then. Not calmer—never calm—but narrower. Focused. The terror did not leave him; it packed itself tightly behind his ribs, giving him something almost like strength.

He looked at his hand as though it belonged to someone else.

His first impulse was revulsion so intense it made him gag. He turned away, squeezing his eyes shut, but the darkness made it worse. In the dark, imagination filled in everything. He opened his eyes again and forced himself to look at the room instead: the damp seam in the wall, the light flicker, the dust gathered beneath the table. Ordinary things. Things that had no opinion about whether he lived or died.

“I can’t,” he said.

The clock answered with another tick.

His mind split in two.

One part begged. It pleaded with him to wait, to think, to find the trick. It spoke in his mother’s voice, in his own voice as a child, in every soft and reasonable tone he had ever trusted.

The other part was cold and merciless. It counted seconds. It measured distance. It reminded him that pain was not the same as death. It told him that if he did nothing, he was choosing something worse.

He began to prepare because preparation was easier than decision.

He stripped off his jacket with clumsy, shaking movements, using his teeth and free hand when the trapped one would not cooperate. He folded the sleeve, then folded it again, making a thick pad. Not enough. Nothing would be enough. Still, he worked at it, because the act of folding cloth felt almost civilized, almost human.

He wiped his palms on his trousers. They were slick with sweat. He flexed his free hand, made a fist, opened it. His fingers trembled so violently they seemed detached from him.

He dragged the tool table closer inch by inch with his foot, each scrape of metal across concrete making him flinch. When it was near enough, he did not touch anything at first. He only stared.

His stomach rolled.

“No,” he whispered. “No, no, no.”

But he took the cloth in his teeth anyway.

That was the moment that broke him: not the pain, not yet, but the knowledge that he had crossed from refusal into ritual. He was arranging himself around the terrible thing. He was becoming the kind of person who could do it.

Tears blurred his vision. He let them. There was no dignity to preserve here, no audience worth lying to. He cried openly, shoulders hitching, breath stuttering around the fabric clenched between his teeth.

Then he forced himself to breathe through his nose.

In for four.

Out for four.

Again.

Again.

He planted his feet flat on the floor. He pressed his back against the chair. He adjusted his grip once, then again, hating the care he was taking, hating the practical part of his mind that insisted precision mattered.

The clock ticked.

He thought of all the small things he had assumed would happen later: returning a call, fixing the kitchen drawer, apologizing to his sister properly instead of with jokes. The future, which had always seemed enormous and vague, had narrowed to the space between his heartbeat and his hand.

“I want to live,” he said.

The words surprised him. They came out cracked, almost inaudible, but once spoken they became an order.

His whole body recoiled from what came next. Every instinct screamed against it. He had to gather himself the way a person gathers scattered papers in a storm—breath, grip, posture, will—only to have them torn loose again by panic.

So he stopped trying to be brave.

He let himself be terrified.

He let himself shake.

Then, with the cloth between his teeth and the taste of old cotton on his tongue, he closed his eyes for one final second—not to avoid what he was about to do, but to say goodbye to the part of himself that still believed he could wake up somewhere else.

When he opened them, he moved.

He opened his eyes again and forced himself to look at the room instead: the damp seam in the wall, the light flicker, the dust gathered beneath the table. Ordinary things. Things that had no opinion about whether he lived or died.

“I can’t,” he said.

The clock answered with another tick.

His mind split in two.

One part begged. It pleaded with him to wait, to think, to find the trick. It spoke in his mother’s voice, in his own voice as a child, in every soft and reasonable tone he had ever trusted.

The other part was cold and merciless. It counted seconds. It measured distance. It reminded him that pain was not the same as death. It told him that if he did nothing, he was choosing something worse.

He began to prepare because preparation was easier than decision.

He stripped off his jacket with clumsy, shaking movements, using his teeth and free hand when the trapped one would not cooperate. He folded the sleeve, then folded it again, making a thick pad. Not enough. Nothing would be enough. Still, he worked at it, because the act of folding cloth felt almost civilized, almost human.

He wiped his palms on his trousers. They were slick with sweat. He flexed his free hand, made a fist, opened it. His fingers trembled so violently they seemed detached from him.

He dragged the tool table closer inch by inch with his foot, each scrape of metal across concrete making him flinch. When it was near enough, he did not touch anything at first. He only stared.

His stomach rolled.

“No,” he whispered. “No, no, no.”

But he took the cloth in his teeth anyway.

That was the moment that broke him: not the pain, not yet, but the knowledge that he had crossed from refusal into ritual. He was arranging himself around the terrible thing. He was becoming the kind of person who could do it.

Tears blurred his vision. He let them. There was no dignity to preserve here, no audience worth lying to. He cried openly, shoulders hitching, breath stuttering around the fabric clenched between his teeth.

Then he forced himself to breathe through his nose.

In for four.

Out for four.

Again.

Again.

He planted his feet flat on the floor. He pressed his back against the chair. He adjusted his grip once, then again, hating the care he was taking, hating the practical part of his mind that insisted precision mattered.

The clock ticked.

He thought of all the small things he had assumed would happen later: returning a call, fixing the kitchen drawer, apologizing to his sister properly instead of with jokes. The future, which had always seemed enormous and vague, had narrowed to the space between his heartbeat and his hand.

“I want to live,” he said.

The words surprised him. They came out cracked, almost inaudible, but once spoken they became an order.

His whole body recoiled from what came next. Every instinct screamed against it. He had to gather himself the way a person gathers scattered papers in a storm—breath, grip, posture, will—only to have them torn loose again by panic.

So he stopped trying to be brave.

He let himself be terrified.

He let himself shake.

Then, with the cloth between his teeth and the taste of old cotton on his tongue, he closed his eyes for one final second—not to avoid what he was about to do, but to say goodbye to the part of himself that still believed he could wake up somewhere else.

When he opened them, he moved.

The deck had gone silent except for the creak of rope and timber.

Captain Marlow stood near the rail, coat snapping in the wind, one gloved hand resting on the hilt of his cutlass. Before him, lashed at the wrists, stood Dorian Vale—the man who had whispered rebellion into the crew’s ears and reached for the captain’s cabin keys before dawn.

“You wanted my ship,” Marlow said, voice low enough that every sailor strained to hear it. “You’ll have the sea instead.”

Two men dragged the plank into place. It jutted out over the water like a narrow finger pointing toward judgment. Below, the ocean rolled dark and glassy, broken by flashes of pale bellies and sharp fins.

Sharks.

They circled the ship with patient hunger, gliding in slow, tightening loops. One broke the surface, its back slick and black beneath the sun, before vanishing again into the blue. Another turned sideways, and for an instant its cold eye caught the light.

Dorian saw them.

All the defiance drained from his face.

“No,” he whispered. Then louder: “Captain—Marlow—please. I was a fool. I’ll take the lash. I’ll take irons. Put me ashore on any cursed rock, but don’t—”

Marlow gave no answer.

The crew watched with hard faces, though a few looked away when Dorian’s boots were set upon the plank. The wood bent under his weight and trembled with the motion of the sea. He stared down, chest heaving, sweat standing out on his brow despite the cool wind.

The sharks below seemed to sense him. Their circles tightened. A fin cut across the surface directly beneath the plank, then another, then three more.

“Walk,” said the captain.

Dorian shook his head, eyes wide and shining. “I can’t.”

“You could raise a blade against me,” Marlow said. “You can take one step.”

The mutineer’s bound hands clenched. His knees nearly gave way. Behind him, a sailor prodded the air with a pike—not touching, not yet, but close enough.

Dorian took one step.

The plank groaned.

He took another, breathing in ragged gasps. Below, the water churned. A shark’s fin sliced past, close enough that spray flicked upward like thrown glass.

“Please,” Dorian sobbed. “Please…”

At the end of the plank, he turned back, pleading with every face on deck and finding mercy in none. The ship rose on a swell. The plank dipped.

For one suspended heartbeat, Dorian stood against the endless sea, pale and shaking.

Then the captain removed his hat.

“May the deep judge you fairer than I.”

The plank lurched beneath Dorian’s feet. His cry tore across the deck as he fell, swallowed by wind, water, and the circling shadows below.

results.model_response:
The first thing they felt was pressure: a hard, unfamiliar weight cinched tight against their ribs, refusing to move when they tried to breathe.

Their hands went to it on instinct and found edges, straps, a cold plastic casing pressed flat against their shirt. Then the wires—thin, rubbery strands looped and bundled beneath their trembling fingers. Some were smooth as shoelaces, others ridged where tape had been wound around them. They slid against the pads of their fingers with a faint, sickening tackiness, and every touch made their stomach twist harder.

Then came the sound.

Tick.

Small. Precise. Intimate.

Tick.

It wasn’t loud, but it seemed to fill their skull, sharper than their own breathing. Their lungs hitched. The straps bit into their shoulders as they tried to pull away from their own body, as if panic alone could create distance between their skin and the thing fastened to them.

“No—no, no, no—”

Their voice cracked into a whisper, then rose too quickly, fraying at the edges. Their fingers hovered over the wires, afraid to touch, afraid not to touch. The device shifted slightly with each ragged breath, its weight thudding against their sternum like a second, mechanical heart.

Tick.

They could feel sweat gathering under the straps, making the fabric cling. Their palms were slick now, useless, trembling so badly that the wires seemed to tremble too. A hysterical laugh burst out of them—one sharp, disbelieving sound—before collapsing into a sob.

They tried to stand still. Tried to think.

But the ticking kept counting through the silence, patient and merciless, while their pulse hammered faster and faster beneath it.

results.model_response:
The hallway had changed in the dark.

In daylight it was narrow and ordinary, a strip of beige carpet between family photos and a leaning bookshelf. At night, with the power out and the rain dragging its nails down the windows, it seemed longer than it should have been. The ceiling pressed low. The doorways stood open like mouths.

Mara kept one hand on the wall and the other out in front of her, fingers spread, trying not to breathe too loudly.

“Ben?” she called.

Her voice came back small.

The house answered with a tick from the baseboard heater, then another from somewhere behind her. Old wood settling. Pipes cooling. Things that had always made noise and never mattered until now.

She swallowed.

The electricity had cut out twenty minutes ago. The storm, she’d told herself. The old transformer at the end of the street, probably. She’d gone for the flashlight in the kitchen drawer and found it empty. She’d laughed then, once, sharply, because of course the batteries were dead. Because of course her phone had been on six percent and now showed only a black, unresponsive screen.

Then she had heard the sound upstairs.

Not a crash. Not anything dramatic.

A footstep.

Just one.

She had stood in the kitchen, hand still inside the junk drawer, listening so hard her ears seemed to ache.

The second step had come after a long pause.

Now she was in the hall.

“Ben, if this is you, it’s not funny.” Her whisper frayed halfway through.

Ben was not home. She knew he was not home. His car was gone. He had texted from the highway an hour ago, delayed by the rain. But saying his name made the house feel less empty. It made the dark seem like something she could reason with.

Her toe struck the edge of the runner and she lurched forward, shoulder bumping the wall. The impact knocked a picture frame crooked. She caught it before it fell, palm slapping glass.

The sound was too loud.

She froze.

At the far end of the hall, the living room sat in a murk of faint gray light leaking through the curtains. Shapes emerged slowly: the back of the couch, the lamp by the armchair, the low table with its bowl of keys. Rain pulsed against the windows, blurring the glass, turning the outside world into silver streaks.

Nothing moved.

Mara eased the frame back onto its nail. Her fingers came away dusty.

Behind her, in the doorway to the dining room, a man stood perfectly still.

He had entered through the laundry room window twelve minutes earlier, pushing the loose pane inward with two gloved thumbs. He had cut his sleeve on the latch but not his skin. He had paused in the utility room, listening to the humless house, the rush of rain, the woman moving below.

Now he watched her from less than fifteen feet away.

The knife was angled down beside his leg, its blade dark except where a thin line of window-light found the edge.

Mara took another step toward the living room.

The man shifted his weight.

The floorboard under his heel gave a soft complaint.

Mara stopped.

Every muscle in her body locked at once.

For a moment she wasn’t sure she had heard anything at all. The rain filled in the silence, steady and insistent. Her pulse thudded in her ears, mimicking footsteps, confusing her.

She turned her head a little, not enough to look back.

“Hello?”

No answer.

The dining room behind her was a black rectangle. She could feel it there. She could feel the doorway, the empty chairs around the table, the china cabinet with its warped reflection. She could feel the space in a way she never had before, as if the dark had weight and had leaned toward her.

Her hand slid along the wall until it found the light switch. She pressed it.

Nothing.

She pressed it again, harder, uselessly.

A soft breath came from behind her.

Mara’s mouth opened, but no sound came out.

The man did not move now. He had made a mistake with the board. He knew it. He held himself in the shadow of the dining room, shoulder tucked behind the doorframe, knife hidden against his thigh. His face was turned toward her, eyes adjusted to the dark.

She was close enough that he could see the pale oval of her cheek, the white line of her knuckles against the wall.

Mara forced herself forward.

One step. Then another.

Do not run, some instinct told her. If you run, it will know you know.

The thought was absurd and childish, but it kept her moving. Her knees felt loose. Her breath came in shallow sips she tried to swallow down. The living room was only a few feet away. If she reached the coffee table, she could get the keys. The car remote had a panic button. The front door was past the stairs. The neighbor’s porch light was always on. There were houses close enough to hear her scream.

If she could scream.

Behind her, the man stepped out of the dining room.

His socks made no sound on the carpet.

Mara reached the end of the hall and put her hand on the back of the couch to steady herself. The fabric was cold and slightly damp from the open window nearby.

Open window.

She had not left a window open.

The curtain beside the armchair stirred inward with the storm’s breath, lifting and falling like a slow hand.

Mara stared at it.

Then at the black gap where the latch should have been closed.

Something inside her finally gave way.

She grabbed for the bowl of keys.

Her fingers struck ceramic. The bowl skidded across the table and hit the floor with a crack that split the room wide open. Keys scattered beneath the couch, bright little sounds disappearing into shadow.

The man lunged.

Mara bolted blind.

She hit the corner of the coffee table with her shin and went down hard, palms slapping the floor. Pain flared white up her leg. She scrambled, nails catching in the carpet, and heard him behind her now—not hiding, not careful. Fast, controlled steps crossing the room.

The knife struck the coffee table where her hand had been a second before.

Wood splintered.

Mara sucked in air to scream and managed only a broken gasp. She kicked backward, her heel connecting with something solid. The man grunted. The sound was human, close, and that frightened her more than the silence had.

She crawled toward the front hall.

Her hand closed around something cold under the couch.

Keys.

She seized them so hard the teeth bit into her palm.

A shape passed over her. She rolled onto her back and saw him for the first time: no face, just a darker figure against the dark, one arm lifted, rainlight slipping along the knife.

The house seemed to hold its breath.

Then, from outside, headlights swept across the curtains.

White light flooded the room.

For one clear instant Mara saw the intruder’s eyes widen.

A car door slammed in the driveway.

“Mara?” Ben’s voice called through the rain.

The man hesitated.

Mara found her scream then. It tore out of her, raw and loud enough to shake the house awake.

The soldier is folded into the mud at the bottom of the trench, no longer thinking of orders or the line or the men beside him—only of breath. The gas hangs low and dirty in the confined space, a pale, crawling fog that clings to wool, skin, and the slick trench walls. His eyes stream uncontrollably, swollen and stinging as if ground glass has been rubbed beneath the lids. Every blink drags fire across them.

His first cough is sharp, almost surprised. Then another follows, deeper, tearing up from his chest. Soon he cannot stop. His whole body convulses with it, shoulders jerking, ribs straining, gloved hands clawing at his collar and mask straps as though the air itself has hands around his throat. When he manages to inhale, the breath comes thin and ragged, whistling through a narrowing airway. It feels hot going in, poisonous and metallic, and his lungs reject it with violent spasms.

His mouth fills with spit and mucus. He tries to swallow but gags instead, retching into the mud, strings of saliva hanging from his lips. The coughs become wet, bubbling, each one seeming to drag something loose from deep inside him. He feels as if he is drowning while standing upright—drowning in his own chest. No breath reaches deep enough. Panic floods him faster than the gas: a primal, animal terror that strips away training and rank and language.

Around him, sounds distort. Men shout, but their voices arrive muffled and far away, as though underwater. Boots scrape. Someone is praying. Someone else is screaming for a medic, though the word breaks apart into coughing before it finishes. The soldier tries to answer, tries to call for help, but all that comes out is a hoarse, broken rasp.

His thoughts fracture into simple, desperate fragments: Air. Mask. Mother. Up. Out. Breathe.

The trench that was once cover becomes a trap. The walls press in. The sky above seems impossibly distant, a narrow strip of grey beyond reach. His hands shake so badly he cannot manage the buckles at his throat. His chest heaves with frantic effort, but each breath is smaller than the last, each inhale a burn, each exhale a shuddering cough. He is aware of his own heartbeat hammering in his ears, of the mud soaking through his knees, of the awful certainty that the next breath may not come.

Mentally, he is no longer a soldier in battle. He is a body fighting for air, reduced to terror, confusion, and instinct. Courage, duty, even fear of death become secondary to the overwhelming need to pull one clean breath into ruined lungs.

The room above the restaurant was too quiet for a place that smelled so warmly of garlic and wine.

Below, plates clattered. Someone laughed. A violin played through the speakers, thin and sweet.

Upstairs, nobody touched the food.

Vittorio Bellandi sat at the head of the long table, his hands folded over the silver head of his cane. Across from him stood Marco, still in his raincoat, water dripping from the hem onto the polished floor.

“You’re certain?” Vittorio asked.

Marco didn’t blink. “He met with them twice.”

“The police?”

Marco nodded once. “And he gave them names.”

A long silence settled over the room.

Vittorio looked down at the untouched bowl of olives in front of him. He picked one up, rolled it between his fingers, and set it back down.

“Sal was always nervous,” he said. “Even as a boy. Always looking over his shoulder.”

“He’s looking the other way now,” Marco said.

Vittorio’s eyes lifted.

Marco lowered his gaze. “Forgive me.”

“No,” Vittorio said softly. “You’re right.”

At the far end of the table, Luca shifted in his chair. He was young enough to still look uncomfortable when decisions were made in quiet voices.

Vittorio noticed.

“You have something to say?”

Luca swallowed. “Sal has a family.”

“So did the men whose names he gave away,” Vittorio replied.

No one spoke after that.

Vittorio leaned back, the leather chair creaking beneath him. “There are rules. Not many. But the ones we have are not suggestions.”

Marco nodded. “What do you want done?”

The old man’s expression did not change.

“Sal has been carrying a heavy burden,” Vittorio said. “See that he puts it down.”

Luca’s face went pale.

Marco asked, “Tonight?”

Vittorio turned his head toward the rain-dark window. The city lights trembled in the glass like candles.

“Before morning,” he said. “I don’t want him waking up to another day of worry.”

Marco buttoned his coat. “And if he talks first?”

“He won’t,” Vittorio said.

Marco waited.

Vittorio’s voice dropped, barely above the music rising from downstairs.

“Make sure his appointment is kept. No confusion. No loose ends.”

Marco gave a small nod. “Understood.”

As he turned to leave, Vittorio added, “Marco.”

He stopped at the door.

“Be respectful,” Vittorio said. “He ate at this table.”

Marco looked back once. “Of course.”

The door closed behind him.

Downstairs, the laughter swelled, bright and careless.

Vittorio reached for his wine at last, held the glass up to the light, and stared through the red as if searching for something he already knew was gone.

The coffin had been cramped before the first shovelful fell.

Now it was shrinking.

Each thud above landed like a verdict, dull and heavy, the sound of the world being piled away one layer at a time. Dirt struck the lid in scattered patters at first, then in thick, wet loads that made the wood groan inches from their face. The air seemed to press lower with every impact, warm and stale, full of the sour smell of varnish, damp earth, and their own panicked breath.

They shoved upward with both hands.

Nothing moved.

The lid held firm, not even a tremor beneath their palms, only the awful sensation of weight gathering over it—soil settling, compacting, sealing them in. Their elbows knocked against the narrow sides. Their knees scraped the lining. There was nowhere to turn, nowhere to stretch, nowhere to be anything but trapped.

Their fingers curled into claws.

They raked at the wood until splinters bit beneath their nails. The sound was pitifully small inside the box: scratch, scrape, gasp, scratch. They hammered with their fists until pain flashed through their knuckles, kicked until their heels thudded uselessly against the boards. Above, the muffled shoveling went on, farther and farther away, as if the world itself were receding.

“Help!” they screamed, but the coffin swallowed the word.

The dirt swallowed the coffin.

Their breathing came too fast now, bouncing back hot against their cheeks. The darkness was total, thick enough to feel on the tongue. They clawed again, harder, sobbing, nails tearing, fingertips slick, desperate to make even the smallest mark—some proof that they were there, alive, fighting.

But the wood did not break.

The earth only settled heavier above them.

The bell should have saved him, but it was still twenty seconds away.

He stood in the corner on legs that looked borrowed, knees dipping every time the other man stepped in. His left eye had swollen nearly shut, the skin puffed tight and glossy, purple blooming under the cheekbone like spilled ink. Blood ran from a split at his brow and kept sliding into his good eye, turning the ring lights into red, smeared halos.

The next jab snapped his head back. Not a knockout punch—worse, almost. A cruel, precise thing that found the same ruined place again. His mouthguard flashed between his lips as he gasped, breath coming wet and ragged. The crowd had stopped roaring in rhythm and started making that low, uneasy sound people make when they know they’re watching too much.

Then came the body shot.

A short hook, buried under the elbow.

There was a sound—not loud, not cinematic—just a hard, ugly crack, like a thick branch breaking under a boot. His face changed before the pain even caught up with him. His mouth opened, but no air came. He folded halfway, one glove dropping to his ribs, and the other fighter was already on him, gloves thudding against arms, jaw, temple.

The referee hovered closer.

Blood streaked down the beaten fighter’s cheek and gathered at his chin, dripping onto the canvas in dark spots. His eye blinked uselessly through it, red-rimmed and unfocused. Still he tried to raise his hands. Still he tried to survive the round.

Another punch turned him sideways into the ropes.

They held him up when his body couldn’t.

The parlor was warm, close with coal smoke and the heavy sweetness of wilting lilies. He had only just set the teacup back in its saucer when his hand faltered, fingers loosening as though the porcelain had grown too heavy to hold. The cup rattled once, sharply, and a dark crescent of tea spilled across the lace cloth.

At first he looked merely puzzled. His brows drew together; his lips parted as if to complain of a bitter taste. Then the color began to leave him. It drained from his cheeks in a slow, ghastly retreat, leaving the skin waxen beneath the lamplight. A sheen of perspiration gathered at his temples. He pressed a hand to his stomach, the other clawing blindly at the edge of the table.

“My dear—” he began, but the words snagged in his throat.

His breathing changed. It came thin and fast, a dry little rasp that seemed too small for so large a man. His eyes widened, not with understanding at first, but with animal alarm. The pupils had gone strange in the lamplight, fixed and dark, and a tremor passed through him from shoulder to wrist. The silver spoon beside his saucer chimed as his shaking hand struck it.

She stood motionless by the mantel, watching.

He tried to rise. The chair scraped violently against the carpet, but his knees buckled before he could stand. One hand flew to his collar, tugging at the starched linen as though the room itself had tightened around his throat. A flush mottled his neck, then faded into gray. His mouth worked soundlessly; a thin line of saliva shone at the corner of it.

The tremors worsened. They seized his arms, then his jaw, setting his teeth against each other with a faint clicking sound. He lurched sideways, striking the table with his hip, and the whole tea service shuddered—cups dancing, saucers clattering, the sugar tongs leaping from their dish. His breath came in ragged pulls now, each one harder won than the last.

When he fell, it was not graceful. He hit the carpet on one knee, then both hands, bent double as if in prayer. A strangled groan escaped him. His face twisted with pain, then slackened, then tightened again as another spasm ran through his body. The veins at his temples stood out darkly. His fingers curled into the pile of the rug, gripping and releasing, gripping and releasing.

At last he rolled onto his side, eyes staring toward the hearth. The firelight flickered over his damp forehead, his ashen lips, the violent flutter at his throat. His chest rose unevenly—once, twice—then paused so long that the ticking clock seemed to grow louder in the silence.

The woman did not move until the teaspoon stopped trembling against the saucer.

The arena had once been a train station.

You could still see the old departure board hanging above the western stands, its black tiles frozen mid-flutter, promising cities no one was allowed to visit anymore. Now the rails had been torn out and the platforms caged over with welded mesh. Floodlights dangled from rusted girders. Loudspeakers crackled with the Ministry anthem until the crowd stopped murmuring.

On the far side of the wire, the ration crates waited in neat gray stacks.

Rice. Salt. Protein bricks stamped with the seal of the Governor.

Enough to keep one district alive for a week.

Mara stood barefoot on the concrete floor, a short iron bar slick in her hand. Across from her, Tomas from Block Nine gripped a chipped machete. He looked thinner than she remembered. Everyone did now. His cheeks were hollow, his prison-issue shirt hanging off him like laundry on a line.

Above them, an official in a white coat raised a gloved hand.

“Citizens,” his voice boomed, magnified and metallic. “Survival belongs to the loyal. Rations belong to the strong.”

The crowd did not cheer. They had learned long ago that silence was safer.

The bell rang.

Tomas moved first, desperate and fast. The machete flashed under the lights, striking sparks from the concrete as Mara twisted away. She felt the wind of it near her ribs. Around them the arena cameras hummed, black glass eyes drinking in every flinch for the evening broadcast.

Mara backed toward an old track trench filled with rainwater. Tomas followed, jaw clenched, eyes wet.

“I have two children,” he said, so softly the microphones might not catch it.

Mara told herself it wasn’t murder if she never saw the crash.

That was the first lie, and it steadied her hands more than she liked to admit. The second was that Victor deserved it—not justice, exactly, but balance. He had smiled through the inquiry, smiled when her brother’s name was dragged through mud, smiled when the company called the death an “unfortunate lapse in protocol.” Victor had signed the report that shifted blame onto a man who could no longer defend himself.

For months, Mara had carried grief like a hot coal in her chest. Every ordinary sight seemed obscene: Victor’s silver car in its reserved space, Victor laughing into his phone, Victor buying lilies from the same florist where Mara had once ordered funeral wreaths.

So when she crossed the parking garage after midnight, she framed it as correction. The world had failed to punish him; she was simply closing the gap. If the car failed on a bend, if speed and arrogance did what courts would not, then wasn’t that consequence? Wasn’t that the shape of truth arriving late?

But beneath each justification was a quieter thought: she wanted him afraid. She wanted one impossible second in which Victor understood helplessness.

The next morning, Mara stood by her kitchen window, waiting for sirens.

None came.

At 8:17, her phone rang. An unknown number. She answered without breathing.

“Mara?” Victor’s voice was thin. “I found something wrong with my car before I left. I don’t know who—”

She hung up.

For the first time in months, the hot coal inside her went cold. Not because he had lived, but because she had wanted him not to. That knowledge sat down beside her like a stranger and did not leave.

By noon, Mara was at the police station, her confession folded in her pocket, each step heavier than revenge had ever promised.

The dog came out of the ash like a thing made of ribs and rage.

It had once been someone’s pet, maybe—there was still the ghost of a collar buried in the matted fur at its neck—but whatever name it had known was gone now. Its lips peeled back from yellow teeth. Its eyes locked on the strip of dried meat in Mara’s hand with the same starving focus she felt burning in her own skull.

She hadn’t eaten in two days.

Not really eaten. A mouthful of rainwater from a rusted hubcap. A thumb-sized lump of something she’d pried from a tin and swallowed before she could smell it. Her stomach had stopped growling hours ago and turned into a cold, twisting knot. Every step made her knees shake. Every thought narrowed to food, food, food.

The dog lunged.

Mara barely got her arm up in time. Its weight slammed into her chest and drove her backward into the mud. Teeth snapped inches from her face, hot breath sour with rot and hunger. She jammed her forearm across its throat, screaming as its claws raked at her coat, shredding fabric that had already been more patch than cloth.

The meat flew from her hand.

Both of them saw it land.

For one second the fight changed shape. The dog twisted toward it. Mara grabbed for a broken length of pipe half-buried beside her boot. Her fingers closed around cold metal, and she swung with everything her empty body had left.

The blow didn’t stop the animal. It only made it angrier.

It came back at her in a frenzy, jaws snapping, paws churning mud. Mara kicked, shoved, slipped, went down again. Pain burst across her shoulder as teeth caught cloth and skin beneath. She cried out—not from bravery, not from fury, but from the simple animal terror of being eaten while still alive.

And underneath the terror was something worse.

She still wanted the food.

Even with blood warming her sleeve, even with the dog thrashing against her, even with its eyes wild and frightened and starving like hers, she thought of that strip of meat lying in the dirt. She thought of chewing. Swallowing. Having enough strength to stand tomorrow.

That was what the world had made of them: two desperate creatures in a dead street, fighting over a scrap too small to save either one.

Mara drove her knee up, shoved the pipe between the dog’s jaws, and pushed until it gagged and reeled back. She scrambled on hands and knees, snatched the meat from the mud, and staggered away before it could recover. Behind her, the dog snarled and limped in a ragged circle, too hungry to retreat, too hurt to charge.

Mara pressed the filthy scrap to her mouth.

She hated herself for it.

Then she ate.

It came back at her in a frenzy, jaws snapping, paws churning mud. Mara kicked, shoved, slipped, went down again. Pain burst across her shoulder as teeth caught cloth and skin beneath. She cried out—not from bravery, not from fury, but from the simple animal terror of being eaten while still alive.

And underneath the terror was something worse.

She still wanted the food.

Even with blood warming her sleeve, even with the dog thrashing against her, even with its eyes wild and frightened and starving like hers, she thought of that strip of meat lying in the dirt. She thought of chewing. Swallowing. Having enough strength to stand tomorrow.

That was what the world had made of them: two desperate creatures in a dead street, fighting over a scrap too small to save either one.

Mara drove her knee up, shoved the pipe between the dog’s jaws, and pushed until it gagged and reeled back. She scrambled on hands and knees, snatched the meat from the mud, and staggered away before it could recover. Behind her, the dog snarled and limped in a ragged circle, too hungry to retreat, too hurt to charge.

Mara pressed the filthy scrap to her mouth.

She hated herself for it.

Then she ate.
